issues.description: In the Results, the meta-analytic effect for Opportunity to Connect is reported as nonsignificant (CI includes zero, p = .065). In the Discussion, this same effect is described as 'significantly different from zero.' This is a direct contradiction that reverses the central conclusion for one of the four outcomes and affects how readers interpret the replication of the original connection finding.
issues.quote: the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.description: The Results report a fail-safe number of 3 for Express and 5 for Connect, but the Discussion reports 5 for Express ('only five unreported studies') and 11 for Connect ('low FSN (11 studies)'). These numbers cannot both be correct and the discrepancy undermines confidence in the reported robustness analyses.
issues.quote: These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent original effect size for advantages
issues.description: The original advantageous self-disclosure effect size is reported as -.30 in the Abstract, Results, and Table 1 (β = -.300), but as -.33 in Table 3 and in the Discussion ('vs. -.33'). The value used as the comparison anchor for all effect-size-difference CIs in Table 3 therefore conflicts with the value reported elsewhere, casting doubt on the difference computations.
issues.quote: widely varying and smaller effect sizes than the original (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33)

issues.description: The Methods state every included study collected the CREP-specified minimum of 120 participants 'to ensure adequate statistical power,' yet Table 1 shows five of seven studies had N below 120 (90, 90, 80, 94, 81) and the text itself says sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374. The studies did not meet the claimed minimum, contradicting the power justification.
issues.quote: collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.description: A low fail-safe number indicates a fragile, easily overturned result, not a robust one. The authors interpret a low FSN for Express as grounds for confidence that future studies will replicate the (null) finding, which inverts the meaning of the statistic. Additionally, FSN logic presupposes a significant meta-analytic result; applying it to the nonsignificant Connect effect is conceptually inappropriate.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.description: The meta-analytic Express effect is statistically significant (r = .08, p = .021, CI excludes zero), yet the authors repeatedly characterize it as evidence of 'no effect' or 'lack of an effect,' relying solely on individual studies' nonsignificance. Concluding a null while the pooled estimate is significant is an internally inconsistent interpretation of the meta-analysis.
issues.quote: Even though the effect size meta-analysis revealed that the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero... all individual replications found regression coefficients not significantly different from zero.

issues.description: The authors infer 'the presence of publication bias in the original study' merely because replication effect sizes/prediction intervals were smaller than the original single-study estimate. Smaller replication effects can arise from sampling error, regression to the mean, or moderators; a single original study being larger does not demonstrate publication bias. This causal claim is repeated for multiple outcomes without appropriate bias-detection analyses.
issues.quote: the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study's, all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study

issues.description: The Results report the Connect prediction interval as [-.09, .26], while the Discussion reports it as [-.07, .27]. The mismatched bounds make it impossible to verify the inferential claims drawn from the interval.
issues.quote: supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero

issues.description: The claim of 'adequate statistical power' is asserted without any power analysis, and most individual replications (N = 80–116) are small, with the original itself at N = 80. The authors later acknowledge wide CIs and that comparing effect-size differences requires larger samples, but the design proceeded with samples too small for the inferential goals (e.g., Goal 5 difference tests), leaving most analyses underpowered.
issues.quote: set at 100 for larger studies). All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.description: The authors acknowledge that data handling (missing data, exclusions, composite scoring) was not documented for several studies, and that item-level data were not consistently stored. No attrition, exclusion counts, or missing-data handling procedures are reported, preventing assessment of whether effect estimates were biased by inconsistent data treatment.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent scale and scoring across sites
issues.description: Two replications used a 5-point RSE while others used a 4-point scale, one study altered item order and wording on 4 of 10 RSE items, and the Gordon study apparently summed rather than averaged items. These heterogeneities in the key predictor's measurement were pooled without sensitivity analysis, threatening comparability of effect sizes across sites.
issues.quote: the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed

issues.subcategory: Selection of studies / file drawer within CREP
issues.description: Of 17 'forks' that began the replication, only 7 that met the minimum sample size and posted data/results were included. Studies that were begun but not completed or not posted may differ systematically (e.g., smaller or null effects), introducing a selection bias into the meta-analysis that is not addressed beyond a brief mention.
issues.quote: has 17 "forks" representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process... These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results

issues.description: Four outcome variables are tested across seven studies plus meta-analytic and difference tests, with significance interpreted at p < .05 throughout and no correction or pre-specified multiplicity plan reported. Marginal results (e.g., Express p = .021, Connect p = .065) are interpreted as meaningful without accounting for the number of tests.
issues.quote: the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero

issues.description: The Connect and Express constructs are each measured with only three items, and the Connect subscale reliability is as low as .68 in some samples. Low reliability attenuates correlations and could partly explain the failure to detect the connection effect, yet this measurement limitation is not weighed when concluding the original finding failed to replicate.
issues.quote: connection: .68 to .84; safety: .84 to .91

issues.subcategory: Overextension to theory and cross-cultural claims
issues.description: Despite a sample limited to U.S. undergraduates at five institutions and only seven small studies, the Discussion advances broad claims about social compensation theory, individualist vs. collectivist cultural differences, and platform-shift (Snapchat/Instagram) explanations. These post hoc speculations far exceed what the correlational, demographically narrow data can support.
issues.quote: In more collectivist cultures, people with lower self-esteem may use Facebook to connect and express themselves to enhance their group membership.

issues.subcategory: Lab vs. online and group administration confounds undocumented
issues.description: Studies varied in administration mode (lab-only, online-only, both) and one site ran participants in groups of two to six. These procedural differences could moderate self-disclosure perceptions, but per-study administration details, counts, and any associated analyses are not fully reported, and the authors decline to test them because each variation occurred in only one or two studies.
issues.quote: three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods). Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six

issues.description: The manuscript claims the statistical methods make it 'an instrumental contribution to replication science,' yet the methods used (random-effects meta-analysis, Anderson & Maxwell effect-size-difference CIs, fail-safe N) are established techniques. The novelty claim overstates the contribution.
issues.quote: the novelty of the statistical methods used to assess the replicability of Forest and Wood (2012) made the present research an instrumental contribution to replication science

issues.description: The project is named the 'Collaborative Replication and Education Project' in the title but the 'Collaborative Research and Education Project (CREP)' in the body. This inconsistency in the central acronym's expansion is a reporting error.
issues.quote: Collaborative Research and Education Project (CREP; Grahe, et al., 2016

issues.subcategory: Heterogeneity statistics from too few studies
issues.description: I-squared and tau-squared estimates (e.g., Safety I2 = 71.76%) are reported with wide CIs from only seven studies, a context the authors themselves note produces biased heterogeneity estimates. Reporting and partially interpreting these statistics (e.g., 'some evidence of heterogeneity') despite acknowledged bias risks misleading readers.

The construct of interest (perceived benefits of Facebook vs. FTF) may have shifted meaning between the 2012 original and 2016–2017 replications because participants likely implicitly compared Facebook to Snapchat/Instagram. The authors raise this as a post hoc explanation but did not measure or control alternative-platform salience, undermining construct comparability with the original.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others

issues.subcategory: Equating standardized beta with effect size r without qualification
issues.description: The note states 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.' This equality holds only for simple bivariate regression; if any replication included covariates or used the Direct-Plus measures in models, beta would not equal r. The assumption is not verified per study, and one study's regression was recomputed by the authors from raw data without detailing the model specification.
issues.quote: Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.
